extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing literary critics, students of literature and poetry, and thoughtful readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the proper function, tone, methods, and standards of literary criticism (with a section specifically on the study and evaluation of poetry). Advises how critics should judge, what to study, and what errors to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: "A disinterested endeavor to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism's primary aim is disinterestedly to discover and spread the best knowledge and thought; its duty is to establish a current of fresh and true ideas rather than to serve immediate practical or party ends. This definition grounds the critic's choices of subject-matter and method throughout the essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness and detachment from practical life
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must keep out of the region of immediate practice in political, social, and humanitarian spheres and embrace a disinterested, detached viewpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By 'eluding sterile conflict' and adopting a detached stance (the author invokes the 'Indian virtue of detachment'), the critic avoids partisanship and can address higher conceptual and ideal questions. Practical entanglement tends to make criticism petty, defensive, or merely tactical; the critic must remain collected and refuse to lend himself to the practical man's point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept slow and indirect effect as the critic's proper work
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism's influence is often subtle, slow, and obscure rather than immediate and practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic must be prepared for a work that progresses gradually—'Slow and obscure it may be, but it is the only proper work of criticism.' The critic's refusal to be practical may reduce immediate influence but gives a chance of admitting wider conceptions into public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain independence from the practical spirit and not praise works merely for utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Even well-meant practical efforts (political movements, 'religions of the future', beneficial institutions) must be criticized if they fall short of ideal or impoverish spiritual perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism must express dissatisfaction with works that, though practically useful, are 'impoverishing and limiting' in the ideal sphere (examples: Miss Cobbe's reconstructed religions, British College of Health). Do not applaud a work only because it has good practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use moral and empirical contrasts to expose excessive triumphalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderate triumphalist or self-congratulatory claims by exposing factual or moral counter-examples placed in juxtaposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: juxtaposing exuberant national self-eulogies (Sir Charles Adderley, Mr. Roebuck) with a brief newspaper report of a child murder ('Wragg is in custody') to show how triumphal rhetoric elides grim realities. Such contrasts can soften and correct excessive public boasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and temperament of the critic: sincere, simple, flexible, ardent, ever-widening knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic should be 'sincere, simple, flexible, ardent, ever widening its knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining this right tone helps the critic avoid practical misunderstandings and gain moral authority. The critic should be patient, able to attach to things and withdraw from them, and should pursue knowledge with ardor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convince the practical man by sincerity, not by aligning with his aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Because practical people are poor at fine distinctions, the critic must reassure them of practical intentions or else ultimately convince them through demonstrated sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the critic does not demonstrate sincerity, he risks being misunderstood or accused of disloyalty to a cause. But he should not compromise critical independence merely to placate practical men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize fresh knowledge and comparative learning before abstract judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge—especially fresh and foreign learning—should be the critic's primary concern; judgment often follows as a secondary, accompanying element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic will generally do most good by communicating fresh knowledge and letting judgment 'pass along with it — insensibly, and in the second place.' To approach the standard of 'the best that is known and thought in the world,' critics should possess at least one great foreign literature and be open to works beyond their national horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize comparative and foreign study (Greek, Roman, Eastern, and other modern literatures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic of literature must dwell much on foreign thought and be equipped with knowledge of Greek, Roman, Eastern antiquity, and other nations' literatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because England (or any single nation) is not all the world, much of the best thought will be foreign; familiarity with other literatures prevents parochialism and helps establish a European (or international) standard of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abstraction and tautological judgment; retain a vivid consciousness of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: When criticism becomes merely abstract 'enunciation and detailed application of principles' it risks being tautological and unsatisfactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when applying principles to familiar subjects, never let yourself become abstract; retain an intimate and lively consciousness of the truth of what you say—if this fails, the criticism is likely wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to praise elements needed for spiritual perfection even if they belong to practically harmful powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism must be 'apt to study and praise elements that for the fulness of spiritual perfection are wanted, even though they belong to a power which in the practical sphere may be maleficent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic should discern spiritual value where practical evaluation would condemn it (and vice versa), without playing powers off against each other in practical terms. Example: finding elevating elements in Catholic marriage theory when the Divorce Court is a public disgrace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set a high standard for poetry; regard the idea as primary
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should be conceived highly: 'for poetry ... the idea is everything; the rest is a world of illusion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because poetry 'attaches its emotion to the idea; the idea is the fact,' critics must expect a high order of excellence from poetry to fulfill its large cultural and spiritual destinies. This requires strict judgment and an elevated conception of poetic function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude charlatanism from poetry and criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry (and the order of thought and art) 'charlatanism shall find no entrance'; criticism must not confuse or obliterate distinctions between excellent/inferior or true/untrue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charlatanism obscures important distinctions and must be guarded against consciously. The critic's duty is to keep the poetic sphere 'inviolate and inviolable' against falseness or superficiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge poetry for excellence, soundness, and truth (the best poetry sustains and forms us)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best poetry is 'excellent rather than inferior, sound rather than unsound or only half-sound, true rather than untrue or only half-true,' and is what is needed to form, sustain, and delight a race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear and deep sense of 'the best' should govern poetic reading and evaluation: favor works that achieve high excellence because they will furnish the greatest long-term cultural and spiritual value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the historic and personal fallacies in poetic judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Two frequent mistaken estimates are (1) the historic estimate—overrating a poet because of his stage in a national development—and (2) the personal estimate—overrating because of personal affinity or circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that historical importance or personal resonance can mislead judgment: do not let a poem's role in the development of a national language automatically inflate its poetic value, nor let personal attachment produce exaggerated praise. Hold constant attention to the real, intrinsic poetic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise patience: let ideas mature before trying to enforce them practically
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rush ideas immediately into practical application; allow them to mature and to shape the world more effectively later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic should 'not, as soon as we get an idea or half an idea, be running out with it into the street' but rather cultivate and mature ideas so that they can change public taste and institutions more profoundly over time.
